transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-11-30
Start Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO, SummitPay), Liam O'Connor (Head of ML), Priya Patel (Eng Manager)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we'll kick off in a sec, so quick intro, I'm Maya, I'm the AE, Diego here is our solutions engineer, he'll run through the structured output and tool-calling demo.
[00:09] Aisha: Thanks, Maya. Quick note, we have about 50 minutes, we've got to hop to another meeting at 15:50, just fyi.
[00:14] Maya: Perfect. Diego, over to you.
[00:16] Diego: Great thanks. So what I'll show today — two things: JSON mode/structured output and the function/tool-calling integration. We'll do a live demo in the Console and then show an API snippet.
[00:30] Diego: First slide, um, recap of why enterprises use structured output: deterministic downstream parsing, easier QA and guardrails for compliance, and simpler contract testing with front-end or backend services.
[00:44] Liam: Quick question — when you say deterministic, do you mean strong schema enforcement or just validation post-hoc?
[00:49] Diego: Good question. We provide both. There's schema validation at generation time using JSON Schema-like rules, plus a fallback/repair flow where the model attempts to reformat to schema if it drifts. You can set strict mode which rejects noncompliant responses.
[01:05] Priya: How often does the repair flow trigger? We've seen too many, um, partial outputs in other systems.
[01:12] Diego: It depends on prompt/temperature and the model family; we provide profiles. For typical e2e payments flows — like your transaction metadata — repair triggers < 10% when configured with our recommended prompt templates and low temp.
[01:29] Maya: Also worth calling out Optimize — our console suggests quantization/model variants and batching settings to reduce token cost while maintaining schema fidelity.
[01:38] Aisha: Can you show the Console?
[01:41] Diego: Yep. Switching over — bear with me. (typing) Here is the Redwood Console workspace, live tenant, and I'm opening the Structured Outputs tab. You can see we have a JSON schema uploaded for "settlement_event".
[01:54] Diego: I'll paste a quick example — it's simple: { "type": "object", "properties": {"tx_id": {"type": "string"}, "amount_cents": {"type": "integer"}, "status": {"enum": ["posted","failed"]} }, "required": ["tx_id", "amount_cents"] }
[02:20] Liam: That looks good. Do you enforce types or coerce? We've had strings for numbers show up.
[02:27] Diego: We try to coerce when safe; with strict mode on we will reject strings for integers. There's also an option to run a post-processor hook that will cast types if you trust the mapping.
[02:39] Maya: Diego, maybe show the API flow with function calling to update internal ledger via a webhook?
[02:44] Diego: Sure. I'll demo function-calling where model returns structured JSON, then Redwood can automatically call a registered tool — e.g., our "post_settlement" webhook — or return the payload to your backend.
[02:58] [03:00] Diego: (API copy/paste) So here is the API payload: model: "redwood-instruct-xxl", mode: "json", schema_id: "settlement_event_v1", functions: [{ name: "post_settlement", url: "https://sandbox.summitpay.internal/api/post_settlement", method: "POST" }], prompt: "Extract settlement event from text and return JSON matching schema".
[03:25] Aisha: Security question — if you call our internal webhook, is traffic proxied or do we need to open inbound?
[03:31] Diego: Good call. For hosted we provide a reverse callback connector that initiates from your VPC to Redwood (outbound), so you don't open inbound. For Dedicated or Private, you can run the tool-caller inside your VPC or on-prem to keep traffic internal.
[03:46] Priya: So for SummitPay, because of PCI/workload, we likely want dedicated or private. Any major differences in structured-output features across modes?
[03:54] Diego: Feature parity is high. The only differences are integrations for network setup and KMS key management. Private supports HSM/KMS on customer-managed keys.
[04:07] [04:10] Diego: Back to demo — I'm going to intentionally send a slightly messy user transcript: "Customer: paid $12.34 for order #A-9921, settled at 03/10, status ok". Let's see the model output.
[04:30] [04:30] System: model returns (imperfect transcribed) — { tx_id: "A-9921", amount_cents: "1234", status: "posted" }
[04:40] Diego: Notice amount_cents came back as string; because I have coercion off by default in this tenant, the Console shows a validation warning. I can toggle strict mode to see how Redwood rejects or repairs.
[04:51] [04:51] Diego: Turning strict on — re-run. Model attempts repair and returns a validated object. If it can't, it returns an error payload and we surface it to the SDK with the error code so you can decide rollback.
[05:05] Liam: If it returns an error payload, can we push to a quarantine queue for human review?
[05:11] Diego: Absolutely — you can configure a dead-letter-route or send to S3/your queue with tags.
[05:17] Aisha: Walk me through guardrails — can we stop models from returning PII fields even if prompt contains them?
[05:24] Diego: Yes we have redaction and policy hooks. You can set deny-lists for fields and Redwood will strip or mask fields before returning or calling tools. We also integrate with customer DLP systems via webhook.
[05:36] Priya: What's the latency hit for strict validation + repair?
[05:40] Diego: There's an extra step; typical overhead is 30-120 ms for small JSONs. If you use a heavyweight repair attempt or a second-model-fallback it can be a few hundred ms. We show this in our Console latency breakdown.
[05:55] Maya: Let's demo tool-calling end-to-end — I'll flip to a code sample in the Console.
[06:00] Diego: (typing) Here is a sample JavaScript flow using the SDK: 

fetch('/v1/generate', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Authorization': 'Bearer <key>' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ model: 'redwood-instruct-xxl', mode: 'json', schema_id: 'settlement_event_v1', functions: [{ name: 'post_settlement' }] })
})
.then(res => res.json()).then(r => {
  if (r.tool_called) {
    // Redwood forwarded to registered webhook
  } else if (r.error) {
    // handle validation error
  }
})

[06:35] Liam: If the tool call fails (3xx/5xx), does Redwood retry?
[06:39] Diego: By default we have a retry policy with exponential backoff up to 3 attempts; you can configure that per tool. We also support synchronous and async modes — sync waits for webhook response, async enqueues a job.
[06:52] Aisha: Can we attach an audit trail that shows the raw model output, the validated payload, and the tool-call response? We need this for audit.
[06:59] Diego: Yes, Console stores an audit log for each request: raw tokens, post-processed payloads, and tool responses. Retention is configurable and you can push logs to your cloud storage for long-term retention.
[07:11] [07:11] Maya: Customer question on cost — how does function-calling affect per-token billing?
[07:16] Diego: We bill per-token generated plus a small per-tool-call webhook charge for outbound calls. If you use async tooling and batching, we can amortize costs. Optimize will suggest batching windows if your throughput fits.
[07:30] Priya: Can Optimize suggest schema changes? Like tighter enums to improve fidelity?
[07:36] Diego: It can. Optimize flags high-variance fields and suggests schema adjustments or prompt templates. It also recommends model/quantization pairs for cost vs accuracy.
[07:48] [08:00] Diego: All right I'll run a quick live run where the model returns an object that would normally break the schema and we route it to a tool which returns 200. (running)
[08:15] System: model returned: { tx_id: "A-9921", amount_cents: 1234, status: "posted", note: "Card xxxx" }
[08:24] Diego: You see note contains masked card; Redwood's PII redactor removed exact digits per policy. The post_settlement tool receives the validated payload.
[08:33] Aisha: In Private mode, would the redaction happen on your side or ours?
[08:37] Diego: If you run Private, redaction logic lives in your deployment unless you opt into Redwood-managed policies. So you get determinism and you control keys.
[08:47] Liam: For our pilot, we want to try model families: 1) high-accuracy hosted model, 2) quantized dedicated instance. Can you run both so we can compare latency and schema accuracy?
[08:58] Diego: Yep, we can bench both. We'll also surface token counts and per-request CPU/GPU time in the Console.
[09:07] Priya: Are there existing integrations for our observability stack — we use Datadog and Snowflake for logs.
[09:13] Diego: We have native Datadog metrics and can export JSON logs to Snowflake or S3. You can also use webhooks for eventing.
[09:22] Maya: There's a question in chat about rollback — if a tool call posts a settlement incorrectly, can Redwood do automated compensating actions?
[09:30] Diego: Redwood can do compensating tooling if you define it. We recommend designing idempotent tool endpoints and exposing a reconciliation API. Some customers use our function-calling to trigger a retry-compensate flow.
[09:44] [09:45] Aisha: Let's talk security docs — can you email SOC2, ISO attestation, and your network architecture for hosted callbacks?
[09:52] Maya: Yes, will send. We'll also include a diagram for callback connector and Dedicated/Private networking.
[09:58] Liam: One nit — your Console schema editor stripped a comment in the schema in the demo, possible UI bug?
[10:05] Diego: Thanks, noted. Might be a rendering quirk in this tenant; we'll add as an action item to investigate.
[10:12] Priya: How do we set up RBAC so only certain roles can toggle strict mode?
[10:17] Diego: Console supports RBAC, SSO via SAML, and role permissions for schema edits, deploys, and toggle switches. We'll share the role matrix.
[10:27] Maya: Let's do a short skim of the logs and latency panel to show overhead. (navigates) You can see per-route metrics, tail latency, and a breakdown for validation/repair time.
[10:43] [10:45] Diego: I'm going to also show the SDK debug output. This is what you get in the client — raw model text, the structured payload, and tool call status with timestamps.
[10:58] Aisha: For the pilot, we need to know expected SLOs. Can you propose a baseline?
[11:04] Diego: For hosted-instruct models with JSON mode and strict validation, 95th percentile latency around 180-300 ms for small payloads. For Dedicated quantized models, P95 ~120-250 ms but depends on batching. We'll provide exact numbers once we run your sample.
[11:22] Liam: We'll hand over 24 hours of production-like traffic and two schema variants. We want a bench that shows error rate, latency, and cost per 10k requests.
[11:32] Diego: Sounds good. We'll map that to a pilot scope and baseline.
[11:37] Maya: Okay we're about 40 minutes in, closing window soon — let's capture next steps.
[11:42] Aisha: Quick question on data residency — do you offer EU-only regions for logs and model execution?
[11:48] Diego: Yes, Redwood has regions in EU, NA, and APAC; you can pin execution and logs to a region. Private can be fully on-prem.
[11:58] Priya: For the pilot, we'd prefer a Dedicated tenant in us-east or eu-west depending on where we route traffic.
[12:05] Maya: We'll propose both options in the follow-up email and a cost comparison.
[12:12] Diego: One last demo note — we support schema versioning and rollouts, so you can canary a stricter schema for subset of traffic to measure break rate.
[12:24] Aisha: Good. Thanks both.
[12:27] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll send the PI and security docs and follow up on the sandbox.
[12:32] Liam: Thanks, bye.
